To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intensive glycemic control may be associated with increased mortality in some patients with type 2 diabetes.
intensive glucose-lowering strategies may not reduce CVD risk in patients with type 2 diabetes.

intensive antidiabetes therapies are not recommended for all patients with type 1 or 2 diabetes, and that the risk of hypoglycemia and weight gain must be considered in the context of the benefits of improved glucose control.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the recent clinical trials on the strategies for treating patients suffering with type 2 DM and the risk of cardiovascular disease.
the effects of diabetes and its treatment on CVD.
the effects of the environment on the human body, particularly on the immune system, and with the role of the immune system in the development of disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of the ACCORD and ADVANCE trials should not change current practice for patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes; rather, they should be used as a guide for future research and to help identify the patients who are at greatest risk of hypoglycemia and/or mortality.
the results of recent clinical trials have not provided a definitive answer to how to best treat patients with type 1 diabetes.
the best treatment for patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes remains the same as it was 30 years ago, which is the best possible control of glucose and other cardiovascular risk factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we need to focus on individual patient risk and benefit to optimize outcomes in patients with type-2 diabetes.

the results from recent clinical trials provide new insights into the impact of intensive glycemic control and its effect on cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type II diabetes mellitus, which will be used to develop a new treatment plan for this patient population.
the use of current antihyperglycemic agents can improve glycemic control, and that the use of intensive glucose control will need to be individually tailored to the patient’s risk factors and needs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not treat diabetes in the same way we treat any other chronic disease.
patients with type 1 diabetes should be educated on the importance of maintaining tight glycemic control and the importance of self-management.

the use of intensive antidiabetes therapies should be tailored to individual patients based on patient characteristics, such as age and comorbidities, to achieve optimal glycemic control while reducing the risk of hypoglycemia.
